name: Training data

subjectOf.text: The performance of an AI neural network's learning algorithm during supervised training rises with the quality and quantity of the labelled datasets it is trained on, which ties AI progress directly to micro task work.
subjectOf.abstract: The higher the quality and quantity of such labelled datasets the better the AI neural network's learning algorithm during the supervised training process.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralized Mechanical Turk Through Verified Reputation (2018). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3128900
scope_conditions: supervised training process

subjectOf.text: Existing centralized micro task marketplaces cannot adequately meet the rising demand for high quality labelled AI training data.
subjectOf.abstract: The existing centralized marketplaces for micro task work cannot adequately fulfil the increasing demand for high quality micro task work for AI labelled training datasets.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralized Mechanical Turk Through Verified Reputation (2018). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3128900
scope_conditions: existing centralized marketplaces
demand for high quality AI training datasets

subjectOf.text: Bias in AI systems arises when algorithms incorporate discriminatory practices carried in their training data, and the resulting outputs reveal a profound misalignment between AI operations and societal values, ethics, and norms.
subjectOf.abstract: AI governance does encounter a critical challenge in mitigating biases within AI systems, where biases can inadvertently arise through algorithms incorporating discriminatory practices due to data used in training.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: arises through the training data pathway
observable in deployed systems such as chatbots and screening tools

subjectOf.text: Routing proposals through the Forum and then through Validation Pool review is what allows the input parameters and learning data of AI systems to be governed by expert community consensus, because only vetted and consensus backed data and parameters reach AI development.
subjectOf.abstract: This process involves submitting proposals to the Forum and undergoing Validation Pool review, ensuring that only vetted and consensus-backed data and parameters are utilized in AI development.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: requires an operating DAO with reputation tokens and validation pools
applies to input parameters and training data selection

subjectOf.text: AI learning is degraded by Web2 platforms because their engagement driven algorithms amplify extreme viewpoints and negativity, so the human sentiment and ethics the models absorb from that data are systematically distorted.
subjectOf.abstract: AI learning is afflicted by web2 systems that bring out suboptimal human generated outcomes. WEB2 platforms often amplify extreme viewpoints and negativity due to their engagement-driven algorithms, presenting a distorted view of human sentiment and ethics.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: applies to models trained on unfiltered web and social media data
arises from engagement optimization in Web2 platforms

subjectOf.text: Deep learning models inadvertently learn and amplify whatever biases exist in their training data, so the composition of the training corpus, not the architecture, is the source of unfair or discriminatory outcomes.
subjectOf.abstract: Depending on the data used for training, deep learning models can inadvertently learn and amplify biases present in the training data, potentially leading to unfair or discriminatory outcomes.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: depends on the data used for training

subjectOf.text: Requiring community members to stake reputation tokens in order to validate data quality is what produces robust and reliable training datasets, and this participatory validation improves annotation accuracy while reducing bias.
subjectOf.abstract: Community members stake reputation tokens to validate data quality, ensuring robust and reliable datasets for training AI models. This participatory approach can improve data annotation accuracy and reduce biases.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: training data validation carried out by a reputation staking community

subjectOf.text: A critical unsolved challenge for AI governance is bias mitigation, because biases enter inadvertently when algorithms incorporate discriminatory practices carried in the data used for training.
subjectOf.abstract: AI governance does encounter a critical challenge in mitigating biases within AI systems, where biases can inadvertently arise through algorithms incorporating discriminatory practices due to data used in training.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance Via Web3 Reputation System (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4941807
scope_conditions: where training data embeds discriminatory practices

subjectOf.text: Bias in judicial AI arises because models are trained on historical data that reflect past inequities, and the standard remedy of fairness through unawareness, meaning the omission of protected characteristics such as race, fails because proxy variables continue to correlate with the omitted attribute.
subjectOf.abstract: This bias arises because AI models rely on historical data that reflect past inequities, and even attempts at "fairness through unawareness" (omitting protected characteristics like race) fail due to proxy variables that correlate with bias.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Morgan A. Gray, The Evolving Role of Artificial Intelligence in Law (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5541658
scope_conditions: machine learning models trained on historical judicial data

subjectOf.text: Because AI systems are predominantly developed in the West and trained mostly on Western data, their outputs are liable to carry cultural biases that inadequately represent non-Western cultures and the values inherent in them.
subjectOf.abstract: Such western AI system domination can be further exacerbated through mostly western training data for AI systems. This may lead to cultural biases in AI outputs as non-western cultures and non-western values inherent in such cultures are inadequately represented.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Morgan A. Gray, The Evolving Role of Artificial Intelligence in Law (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5541658
scope_conditions: AI systems deployed in non-Western legal systems
training corpora dominated by Western sources

subjectOf.text: Computational abundance does not eliminate information asymmetry; it transforms its locus, since traditional informational advantages such as knowledge of market conditions, contract terms, and domain expertise become accessible at negligible cost.
subjectOf.abstract: Computational abundance does not eliminate information asymmetry, it transforms its locus. Traditional informational advantages, knowledge of market conditions, understanding of contract terms, possession of domain expertise, become accessible at negligible cost.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Computative Economics A Framework for Economic Analysis under Computational Abundance (2026). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=6607458

subjectOf.text: The paper follows on from the author's Reinforcement Learning from Reputation Feedback paper and tests one use of that mechanism, as a filter on training data, and not the mechanism as a whole.
subjectOf.abstract: Intelligence models increasingly learn from data that earlier Intelligence models produced, and when that loop repeats the rare cases disappear first. This paper preregisters a test of whether a reputation-weighted validator pool, filtering the training data of a recursive replacement loop, keeps those rare cases alive. The outcomes remain sealed until a replication of the original model-collapse result succeeds.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Can Reputation Prevent Model Collapse? A Preregistered Test of Reputation-Weighted Data Filtering (2026). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=7598518
scope_conditions: Scope is relative to the author's parent reputation-feedback paper.
The restriction is the paper's own statement of what it does and does not test.

subjectOf.text: Reputation is settled once by key, after the generation-0 fit on real data and before generation 1, and no candidate that enters training ever updates a reputation.
subjectOf.abstract: Intelligence models increasingly learn from data that earlier Intelligence models produced, and when that loop repeats the rare cases disappear first. This paper preregisters a test of whether a reputation-weighted validator pool, filtering the training data of a recursive replacement loop, keeps those rare cases alive. The outcomes remain sealed until a replication of the original model-collapse result succeeds.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Can Reputation Prevent Model Collapse? A Preregistered Test of Reputation-Weighted Data Filtering (2026). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=7598518
scope_conditions: The design uses only keyed settlement, although the parent rule also covers unkeyed events.
This removes reputation dynamics during the recursion, so the weights are fixed throughout the run.

subjectOf.text: The pool's entire exposure to real data is 192 rows, below the 200 real rows the ten percent arm receives and far below the roughly 1,990 distinct real rows it trains on over the run.
subjectOf.abstract: Intelligence models increasingly learn from data that earlier Intelligence models produced, and when that loop repeats the rare cases disappear first. This paper preregisters a test of whether a reputation-weighted validator pool, filtering the training data of a recursive replacement loop, keeps those rare cases alive. The outcomes remain sealed until a replication of the original model-collapse result succeeds.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Can Reputation Prevent Model Collapse? A Preregistered Test of Reputation-Weighted Data Filtering (2026). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=7598518
scope_conditions: The keyed record is stratified to teach the pool who judges validity well on which tag, and nothing about where the rare components lie beyond a bounded tag leakage.

The source's text layer drops an exponent inline, so the quote renders the formulas as "in one 50 generation" and "N(1 - 0. 9 )". The claim asserts only the three row counts, which the quote states in figures.
